title: Malachi

stories.title: 📜 Malachi 1
summaryBullets: This is the burden of the word of the LORD to Israel through Malachi: (1:1).
“I have loved you,” says the LORD. But you ask, “How have You loved us?” “Was not Esau Jacob’s brother?” declares the LORD. “Yet Jacob I have loved, (1:2).
but Esau I have hated, and I have made his mountains a wasteland and left his inheritance to the desert jackals.” (1:3).

Though Edom may say, “We have been devastated, but we will rebuild the ruins,” this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “They may build, but I will demolish. They will be called the Land of Wickedness, and a people with whom the LORD is indignant forever. (1:4).
You will see this with your own eyes, and you yourselves will say, ‘The LORD is great — even beyond the borders of Israel.’” (1:5).

“A son honors his father, and a servant his master. But if I am a father, where is My honor? And if I am a master, where is your fear of Me?” says the LORD of Hosts to you priests who despise My name. “But you ask, ‘How have we despised Your name?’ (1:6).
By presenting defiled food on My altar. But you ask, ‘How have we defiled You?’ By saying that the table of the LORD is contemptible. (1:7).

When you offer blind animals for sacrifice, is it not wrong? And when you present the lame and sick ones, is it not wrong? Try offering them to your governor! Would he be pleased with you or show you favor?” asks the LORD of Hosts. (1:8).
“But ask now for God’s favor. Will He be gracious? Since this has come from your hands, will He show you favor?” asks the LORD of Hosts. (1:9).

“Oh, that one of you would shut the temple doors, so that you would no longer kindle useless fires on My altar! I take no pleasure in you,” says the LORD of Hosts, “and I will accept no offering from your hands. (1:10).

For My name will be great among the nations, from where the sun rises to where it sets. In every place, incense and pure offerings will be presented in My name, because My name will be great among the nations,” says the LORD of Hosts. (1:11).
“But you profane it when you say, ‘The table of the Lord is defiled, and as for its fruit, its food is contemptible.’ (1:12).

You also say: ‘Oh, what a nuisance!’ And you turn up your nose at it,” says the LORD of Hosts. “You bring offerings that are stolen, lame, or sick! Should I accept these from your hands?” asks the LORD. (1:13).

“But cursed is the deceiver who has an acceptable male in his flock and vows to give it, but sacrifices a defective animal to the Lord. For I am a great King,” says the LORD of Hosts, “and My name is to be feared among the nations. (1:14).
crossRefs: Genesis 25:23: Jacob and Esau distinguished before birth.
Romans 9:10-13: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” cited later.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָהַב / שָׂנֵא (ʾahav / saneʾ), Greek (LXX): ἠγάπησα / ἐμίσησα, Aramaic: רְחִים / סָנֵי
translationNotes.note: Semitic ‘love/hate’ can express choosing/favoring vs. rejecting, not mere emotion. Here it marks God’s covenant choice of Jacob over Esau (1:2-3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְאָכִי (Malʾakhi, ‘my messenger’), Greek (LXX): Μαλαχίας, Aramaic: מַלְאָכִי
translationNotes.note: Could be a personal name or a title meaning ‘my messenger’ (1:1).

The law fixed the standard and named the disqualifiers. Leviticus 22:20-24 rules out any animal that is blind, injured, maimed, or has a running sore, a festering rash or a scab, and Deuteronomy 15:21 repeats the ban on the lame and the blind. A defective beast was worth less at market, so bringing one to the altar meant keeping the sound animal back for yourself. Malachi 1:8 makes the test plain: try handing that animal to your governor and see if he takes it.

Not a local elder. Judah in this period was a small province of the Persian Empire, and the pechah was the man Persia appointed over it, responsible for order and for the tribute. Haggai 1:1 gives the title to Zerubbabel, and Nehemiah 5:14-15 says the governors before him took bread, wine and forty shekels of silver from the people as their allowance. A gift presented to such a man had to be worth having.

Edom is the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's older brother, settled in the rugged highlands south and east of the Dead Sea. The two peoples were at odds for their whole history: Edom refused Israel passage on the King's Highway and came out armed to stop them (Numbers 20:14-21), and Psalm 137:7 remembers Edomites cheering the fall of Jerusalem with the cry to tear it down to its foundations. That is the history behind the mountains left to jackals in Malachi 1:3.

stories.keyTakeaway: God affirms covenant love for Israel and announces Edom’s downfall, showing His rule beyond Israel’s borders.

stories.title: 🕍 Malachi 2
summaryBullets: “And now this decree is for you, O priests: (2:1).

If you do not listen, and if you do not take it to heart to honor My name,” says the LORD of Hosts, “I will send a curse among you, and I will curse your blessings. Yes, I have already begun to curse them, because you are not taking it to heart. (2:2).
Behold, I will rebuke your descendants, and I will spread dung on your faces, the waste from your feasts, and you will be carried off with it. (2:3).
Then you will know that I have sent you this commandment so that My covenant with Levi may continue,” says the LORD of Hosts. (2:4).
“My covenant with him was one of life and peace, which I gave to him; it called for reverence, and he revered Me and stood in awe of My name. (2:5).
True instruction was in his mouth, and nothing false was found on his lips. He walked with Me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity. (2:6).
For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts. (2:7).
But you have departed from the way, and your instruction has caused many to stumble. You have violated the covenant of Levi,” says the LORD of Hosts. (2:8).
“So I in turn have made you despised and humiliated before all the people, because you have not kept My ways, but have shown partiality in matters of the law.” (2:9).
Do we not all have one Father? Did not one God create us? Why then do we break faith with one another so as to profane the covenant of our fathers? (2:10).
Judah has broken faith; an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem. For Judah has profaned the LORD’s beloved sanctuary by marrying the daughter of a foreign god. (2:11).
As for the man who does this, may the LORD cut off from the tents of Jacob everyone who is awake and aware — even if he brings an offering to the LORD of Hosts. (2:12).
And this is another thing you do: You cover the altar of the LORD with tears, with weeping and groaning, because He no longer regards your offerings or receives them gladly from your hands. (2:13).

Yet you ask, “Why?” It is because the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant. (2:14).

Has not the LORD made them one, having a portion of the Spirit? And why one? Because He seeks godly offspring. So guard yourselves in your spirit and do not break faith with the wife of your youth. (2:15).

“For I hate divorce,” says the LORD, the God of Israel. “He who divorces his wife covers his garment with violence,” says the LORD of Hosts. So guard yourselves in your spirit and do not break faith. (2:16).

You have wearied the LORD with your words; yet you ask, “How have we wearied Him?” By saying, “All who do evil are good in the sight of the LORD, and in them He delights,” or, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 33:8-11: Blessing on Levi for teaching and guarding.
Ezekiel 44:15-23: Priests to teach the holy vs. the common.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִוֵּר / פִּסֵּחַ / חוֹלֶה (ʿivver / pisseaḥ / ḥoleh), Greek (LXX): τυφλόν / χωλόν / νοσοῦν, Aramaic: סַמֵּא / חִגֵּר / כֵהֵא
translationNotes.note: Blind, lame, or sick animals were forbidden as sacrifices (1:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית לֵוִי (berit Levi), Greek (LXX): διαθήκη Λευΐ, Aramaic: קְיָמָא דְלֵוִי
translationNotes.note: A ministry covenant marked by fear of God, true teaching, and turning many from sin (2:4-8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּרֶשׁ (peresh, the stomach contents and dung of a sacrificial animal)
translationNotes.note: The offal of a sin offering, the hide, the entrails and the dung, was carried outside the camp and burned on the ash heap; it could not stay near the altar (Exodus 29:14; Leviticus 4:11-12; Leviticus 16:27). Malachi 2:3 takes that waste and puts it on the faces of the priests. The one thing that had to be removed from the sanctuary is smeared on the men who serve in it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְכִסָּה חָמָס עַל־לְבוּשׁוֹ (v'chissah chamas al-levusho)
translationNotes.note: Spreading the edge of your garment over a woman was the gesture that claimed her as wife. Ruth asks Boaz for exactly that in Ruth 3:9, and Ezekiel 16:8 uses it of the LORD covering Israel and entering a covenant with her. Malachi says the same garment comes back covered in violence. Deuteronomy 24:1-4 is the law he is speaking against, which allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and send his wife away.

stories.keyTakeaway: God rejects corrupt worship and warns priests who profane His name and twist instruction; His covenant with Levi required truth and reverence.

stories.title: 🔥 Malachi 3
summaryBullets: “Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me. Then the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple — the Messenger of the covenant, in whom you delight — see, He is coming,” says the LORD of Hosts. (3:1).
But who can endure the day of His coming? And who can stand when He appears? For He will be like a refiner’s fire, like a launderer’s soap. (3:2).
And He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver; He will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver. Then they will present offerings to the LORD in righteousness. (3:3).
Then the offerings of Judah and Jerusalem will please the LORD, as in days of old and years gone by. (3:4).

“Then I will draw near to you for judgment. And I will be a swift witness against sorcerers and adulterers and perjurers, against oppressors of the widowed and fatherless, and against those who defraud laborers of their wages and deny justice to the foreigner but do not fear Me,” says the LORD of Hosts. (3:5).
“Because I, the LORD, do not change, you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed. (3:6).

Yet from the days of your fathers, you have turned away from My statutes and have not kept them. Return to Me, and I will return to you,” says the LORD of Hosts. “But you ask, ‘How can we return?’ (3:7).
Will a man rob God? Yet you are robbing Me! But you ask, ‘How do we rob You?’ In tithes and offerings. (3:8).
You are cursed with a curse, yet you— the whole nation— are still robbing Me. (3:9).

Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house. Test Me in this,” says the LORD of Hosts. “See if I will not open the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing without measure. (3:10).
I will rebuke the devourer for you, so that it will not destroy the fruits of your land, and the vine in your field will not fail to produce fruit,” says the LORD of Hosts. (3:11).
“Then all the nations will call you blessed, for you will be a land of delight,” says the LORD of Hosts. (3:12).
“Your words against Me have been harsh,” says the LORD. “Yet you ask, ‘What have we spoken against You?’ (3:13).
You have said, ‘It is futile to serve God. What have we gained by keeping His requirements and walking mournfully before the LORD of Hosts? (3:14).
So now we call the arrogant blessed. Not only do evildoers prosper, they even test God and escape.’” (3:15).

At that time those who feared the LORD spoke with one another, and the LORD listened and heard them. So a scroll of remembrance was written before Him regarding those who feared the LORD and honored His name. (3:16).
“They will be Mine,” says the LORD of Hosts, “on the day when I prepare My treasured possession. And I will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves him. (3:17).
So you will again distinguish between the righteous and the wicked, between those who serve God and those who do not.” (3:18).
crossRefs: Isaiah 40:3: A voice preparing the way.
Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2: Applied to John the Baptist and the Lord’s coming.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְאָךְ (malʾakh), Greek (LXX): ἄγγελος, Aramaic: מַלְאָכָא
translationNotes.note: Same word can mean ‘messenger’ or ‘angel’; Malachi’s name also means ‘my messenger’ (3:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵשׁ מְצָרֵף / בֹּרִית מְכַבְּסִים, Greek (LXX): πῦρ χωνευτηρίου / σμηκτῆρες, Aramaic: נוּרָא דְמְצָרְפִין / בּוֹרִית
translationNotes.note: Images of cleansing precious metal and laundering cloth (3:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲשֵׂר (ma'aser, a tenth) - בֵּית הָאוֹצָר (beit ha-otsar, the storehouse)
translationNotes.note: The tithe was a tenth of the harvest and of every tenth animal passing under the shepherd's rod (Leviticus 27:30-32), and it was the Levites' entire income, given to them in place of tribal land (Numbers 18:21-24). The storehouse was the set of temple storerooms that held the grain, new wine and oil. Nehemiah 13:10-12 records what an empty storehouse actually did: the Levites and singers walked off their posts and went back to their own fields to eat.

A royal record of services performed, kept so that the king could reward them later. Esther 6:1-3 shows one in use: a sleepless Persian king has the Book of Records read to him, finds that Mordecai exposed an assassination plot, and asks what honor was ever given him. Malachi 3:16 describes such a book written before the LORD, listing those who feared Him and honored His name.

stories.keyTakeaway: God answers charges of injustice: His messenger prepares the way, the Lord comes to His temple to purify and to judge, and His unchanging character explains Israel’s survival.

stories.title: 🌅 Malachi 4
summaryBullets: “For behold, the day is coming, burning like a furnace, when all the arrogant and every evildoer will be stubble; the day is coming when I will set them ablaze,” says the LORD of Hosts. “Not a root or branch will be left to them.” (4:1).
“But for you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and you will go out and leap like calves from the stall. (4:2).
Then you will trample the wicked, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet on the day I am preparing,” says the LORD of Hosts. (4:3).
“Remember the law of My servant Moses, the statutes and ordinances I commanded him for all Israel at Horeb. (4:4).
Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD. (4:5).
And he will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers. Otherwise, I will come and strike the land with a curse.” (4:6).
crossRefs: Exodus 32:32-33: Names written in God’s book.
Joel 2:31: Great and terrible day of the LORD.
Luke 1:16-17: John the Baptist in the spirit and power of Elijah.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר זִכָּרוֹן (sefer zikkaron), Greek (LXX): βιβλίον μνημοσύνης, Aramaic: סִפְרָא דִדְכוֹרָנָא
translationNotes.note: Record of those who fear the LORD and esteem His name (3:16).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁמֶשׁ צְדָקָה (shemesh tsedaqah), Greek (LXX): ἥλιος δικαιοσύνης, Aramaic: שִׁמְשָׁא דִצְדָקָא
translationNotes.note: Image of life-giving light and healing for those who fear God (4:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵלִיָּהוּ (ʾEliyahu), Greek (LXX): Ἠλίας, Aramaic: אֵלִיָּה
translationNotes.note: A promised prophetic figure preceding the day of the LORD (4:5-6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵרֶם (ḥerem), Greek (LXX): ἀνάθεμα / ἀφανισμός, Aramaic: חֵרֶם
translationNotes.note: A devoted ban or total destruction; the warning that closes the book (4:6).

stories.keyTakeaway: God records the names of those who fear Him, promises a burning day for evildoers and healing for those who fear His name, commands remembrance of Moses’ law, and promises Elijah before the great day.

intro:
Malachi was written by Malachi (Malachi 1:1), the prophet whose name in Hebrew (Malakhi, מַלְאָכִי) means "my messenger," from the noun malakh ("messenger" or "angel") with the first-person possessive suffix. The book was composed around 430 BC, during or shortly after the second governorship of Nehemiah in Jerusalem (Nehemiah's first governorship: 445-433 BC; his return to Persia and probable second governorship: late 430s BC). The specific religious and social abuses that Malachi denounces - blemished sacrifices, the corruption of the priesthood, divorce, intermarriage with foreign wives, and the withholding of tithes - correspond exactly to the abuses that Nehemiah found and reformed during his second governorship (Nehemiah 13:1-31), confirming the dating. Malachi ministered to the post-exilic community in Jerusalem under Persian rule, approximately a century after the rebuilding of the second temple in 516 BC. Of Malachi's personal background, Scripture preserves nothing beyond his name. He is regarded in Jewish tradition as the last of the Old Testament prophets; after Malachi's ministry, the tradition holds that "the Holy Spirit departed from Israel" (preserved in Tosefta Sotah 13:2), beginning the roughly four-hundred-year period of prophetic silence that ended with the ministry of John the Baptist, the very forerunner whom Malachi himself foretold (Malachi 3:1 and Malachi 4:5-6).

The historical setting is the late Persian period under the reign of Artaxerxes I (465-424 BC), more than a century after the first return from Babylonian exile and a generation after Ezra's reforms and the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah. The returned community had settled into the routines of Persian provincial life: paying tribute to Persia, conducting trade with neighboring provinces (Idumea to the south, Samaria to the north, Ammon to the east), and worshipping at the second temple. The temple was now nearly a century old, the immediate hardship of the resettlement was long past, and a complacent religious formalism had set in. Malachi's contemporaries included the elderly Nehemiah completing his reform work in Jerusalem, the Persian governor of the satrapy of Trans-Euphrates, and possibly the scribe Ezra in his last years. Beyond Judah's borders, the Persian Empire was beginning its decline: the Greco-Persian Wars had ended with Persian defeats at Plataea (479 BC) and Eurymedon (466 BC), and the Athenian-led Delian League dominated the Aegean; Egypt was in periodic revolt against Persian rule and would briefly regain independence under the 28th Dynasty in 404 BC; Sparta and Athens were locked in the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BC) in mainland Greece. Within decades of Malachi's writing, Socrates would teach in Athens (470-399 BC) and Greek philosophy would take its classical form.

Malachi is the thirty-ninth and final book of the Christian Old Testament and the twelfth and last of the twelve Minor Prophets. The Hebrew name Malakhi (מַלְאָכִי) is the prophet's own name. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Malachi were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; the earliest copies date to the 2nd century BC. Malachi closes with a prophecy that the prophet Elijah would return before "the great and awesome day of YHWH" (Malachi 4:5-6); Jesus identified this prophecy as fulfilled by the ministry of John the Baptist (Matthew 11:14; 17:10-13; Mark 9:11-13), and Luke 1:17 records the angel Gabriel announcing John's birth as the fulfillment of Malachi's prophecy. Malachi 3:1 ("Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me") is also quoted in Matthew 11:10, Mark 1:2, and Luke 7:27 as fulfilled by John the Baptist's ministry. Romans 9:13 quotes Malachi 1:2-3 ("Jacob have I loved, Esau have I hated") in Paul's discussion of God's sovereign election.
